newsitem.title: USA: US CFTC's Born--agency has enough crisis authority.
newsitem.headline: US CFTC's Born--agency has enough crisis authority.

text.p: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission had sufficient surveillance and enforcement authority to cope with the Sumitomo Corp copper market crisis, the commission's chairwoman said Wednesday.

Brooksley Born, in her first testimony to Congress as head of the commission, resisted calls by some legislators to give the CFTC more power in the wake of Sumitomo's $1.8 billion loss that rocked world copper markets.

"The CFTC's surveillance system not only provided an early warning of potential problems in the copper market, but also permitted the commission quickly to assess potential risks to U.S. markets," Born said in prepared remarks for a House Banking Committee hearing.
Born declined to discuss details of the commission's investigation into world copper markets, but said the probe is ongoing and make take some time to complete.

Born said the CFTC is coordinating its efforts with the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and regulators in the United Kingdom and Japan.

If Sumitomo had done its copper trading on U.S. markets, the CFTC would have had even more information under large trader reporting requirements, speculative position limits and other constraints, Born said.
Most of Sumitomo's trading was conducted at the London Metal Exchange. LME officials declined an invitation to appear at the Banking Committee hearing.
Cooperation among regulators in different countries during crises like the Sumitomo situation could be improved, Born said.

"Issues concerning the scope and relevancy of requested information can delay the ability of the commission to obtain needed surveillance information," Born said. "We have concluded that addressing these issues in advance of a crisis would help to eliminate delays in the future."
